title: New editor in keyboard manager doesn't distinguish properly between "duplicate" keys on a keyboard
author: sonix1977nl
summary: The new Keyboard Manager editor collapses physically distinct keys that share the same display text, and current key-mapping code round-trips several new-editor paths through GetKeyCodeFromName(name), which returns the first matching key name only.

judgment.rationale: The public repro is precise, and current Keyboard Manager source shows a concrete identity-loss path: duplicate physical keys are converted to display names and then resolved back to a single key code by name lookup.
evidence: The issue describes a specific hardware case with two backslash keys where the old editor distinguishes the keys but the new editor always resolves both to the right-hand key.
src/common/interop/keyboard_layout.cpp implements LayoutMap::GetKeyFromName() by iterating GetKeyNameList(false) and returning the first key whose display name matches the supplied string.

src/modules/keyboardmanager/KeyboardManagerEditorUI/Interop/KeyboardMappingService.cs exposes GetKeyCodeFromName(string keyName), and multiple new-editor validation/update paths call that method when rehydrating selected keys.

src/modules/keyboardmanager/KeyboardManagerEditorLibrary/KeyDropDownControl.cpp stores a numeric SelectedValue for ComboBox selections, but text-based paths still fall back to GetKeyFromName(text), which collapses duplicate-name keys to one identity.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve a focused Keyboard Manager fix that keeps a stable key identity through the new editor and only uses display names for presentation.

fix_assessment.rationale: No linked fix attempt is visible, and the new-editor code already shows a narrow root-cause path for duplicate-name keys.

issue_context.summary: A keyboard with two different backslash keys exposes that the new Keyboard Manager editor no longer preserves the identity of keys that share the same display name.
known_information: The report is on PowerToys 0.100.2 from the Microsoft Store and names a Logitech Silent Wireless Combo MK295 as the affected keyboard.
The reporter says the old editor could distinguish the two keys both by physical key detection and by dropdown selection.
The new editor instead resolves both physical keys to the same right-side key and even selecting the other dropdown entry snaps back to the same identity.
The issue was later assigned to niels9001, but no public fix or workaround is linked.
inferences: The regression is in the new editor's identity handling rather than in Windows keyboard layout data alone, because the old editor reportedly distinguished the same hardware successfully.
Any path that serializes selected keys only as display names is likely to reproduce this class of bug for other duplicate-name keys as well.
issue_context.analysis: This is ready for a design/start decision. The current code shows exactly how the new editor can lose key identity when two distinct codes share one visible label.
initial_investigation: src/common/interop/keyboard_layout.cpp resolves key names back to codes by first-match name lookup, which cannot uniquely represent two distinct keys that render with the same visible text.
src/modules/keyboardmanager/KeyboardManagerEditorUI/Interop/KeyboardMappingService.cs and related validation code repeatedly convert between key names and key codes in the new editor.

src/modules/keyboardmanager/KeyboardManagerEditorLibrary/KeyDropDownControl.cpp shows that dropdown selections have a numeric value available already, which suggests the bug is in later text-based round-tripping rather than in raw UI selection alone.

actions.label: Approve duplicate-key identity fix
actions.note: High-confidence Keyboard Manager regression: the new editor is losing stable key identity when duplicate display names map back through first-match name lookup.

proposed_fixes.title: Preserve stable key identity for duplicate-name keys in the new editor
proposed_fixes.root_cause: The new Keyboard Manager editor round-trips selected keys through human-readable key names, but LayoutMap::GetKeyFromName() returns only the first matching key for a given display label, so two distinct physical keys with the same label collapse to one identity.
plan: Keep the selected key identity as a stable key code or a richer key identity (for example, code plus scan-code-specific metadata where needed) throughout the new editor pipeline instead of rehydrating from display text alone.
Update duplicate-name rendering so dropdown rows remain distinguishable to the user when two different keys share the same visible character or name.
Add regression coverage for keyboards with duplicate-name keys so the new editor preserves separate left/right or OEM key identities across selection, save, and reload.
verification: On affected hardware, map the left backslash key and confirm the new editor does not silently switch it to the right backslash key.
Reload the saved remap and verify both duplicate-name keys remain distinct in the UI and in the resulting mapping.

confidence.rationale: The public repro is very specific, and the current name-to-key first-match lookup explains both the wrong-key selection and the dropdown snapping behavior directly.
